identity-operations.text: Every operation, one by one: what the earlier deployed validators (version 1) did, and what the M1 return replaces it with.

The Shipped today sections describe the version 1 programs published on preprod on 2026-07-28 and exercised by settled transactions; their validators are no longer in the source tree. The Under the accepted design sections describe the accepted design, defined in lean/CardanoKeri/Checkpoint.lean, proved in CheckpointGoals.lean and playable in the checkpoint simulator. The source tree implements part of it (there is no poison spend yet); none of it is claimed deployed. For evidence and transaction IDs, start with the story ladder.

A KERI AID (Key Event Receipt Infrastructure Autonomic Identifier) has a signed KEL (Key Event Log). cardano-keri does not put the whole KEL on Cardano. It stores one current checkpoint in a sovereign UTxO (unspent transaction output) identified by a quantity-one token derived from the AID.

the-datum.text: In the earlier deployed design, CheckpointDatumV1 was pure key state — nine fields, no lifecycle flag (the record was removed from onchain/lib/cardano_keri/checkpoint/datum.ak in 7c49bd97):
current controller public keys and their weighted threshold;
commitments to the next controller keys and their next threshold;
the current KERI witness set and its threshold, called toad;
Lifecycle state lives outside it, in the script role address the token sits at.

Datum V2, in the accepted design, adds what the new machine needs: the epoch, poisoned (the owner's own lock on the checkpoint), frozen, born_at (for juvenility: the age a checkpoint must reach before a consumer trusts it), refund_to and the top-up mark. The model has no checkpoint expiry field. The three sums of money — D_reg the conviction bond, B the freeze bond and the pool of advance funds — are value, not fields. The version 2 datum is written by the validator in the source tree (onchain/lib/cardano_keri/checkpoint/datum.ak).

shipped-today.text: Registration is permissionless: anyone may relay a public KERI inception and fund the escrow. The inception itself determines the keys; the relayer cannot substitute different controller authority. It has two transactions.

1. BLAKE3 premint. The KERI AID is a BLAKE3 digest of the inception bytes in KERI's saidification form. Plutus has no native BLAKE3 builtin, so a dedicated Aiken policy performs that expensive check and mints a deterministic proof token. The token records one fact — the supplied inception bytes have the supplied KERI AID — and grants no identity authority.
2. Checkpoint mint. In the deployed generation the checkpoint transaction (the registry generation books, folds and returns instead, see Register in a registry):
uses the bare mint redeemer Register;
includes a zero-lovelace withdrawal from the registration observer;
puts the complete RegistrationEvidence in that observer's envelope;
consumes an input carrying the matching proof token and burns it;
verifies the inception's controller signatures and witness receipts over the exact event bytes;
verifies that the new datum projects the event's AID, keys, thresholds, next commitments, witnesses, and toad;
mints exactly one AID-derived checkpoint token; and
creates exactly one output holding the token and the required escrow.
The checkpoint and observer programs are delivered by reference; the evidence is not duplicated in the mint redeemer. See Observer architecture.

The duplicate-registration residual. Registration uses no shared registry and no absence proof, so two independent transactions can mint live candidates for the same AID. A consumer must resolve exactly one and fail closed on zero or several — and it cannot prove no other exists. A holder of some retired epoch's keys can therefore mint a rival checkpoint and advance it exactly to their epoch.

under-the-accepted-design.text: Registration becomes a request against the registry: it identifies the AID and carries the bonds and a refund address chosen by whoever pays. The constitution requires the controller's booking to validate the inception evidence, and the application mint now does: it verifies the inception at the booking, through an attestation minted in the same transaction. The registry's folder applies the request in a batch, needs nothing from the controller and reads no inception evidence. This does not require the raw inception to be stored in the request: the attestation authenticates the inception's validity and its initial key state. An identifier may be booked more than once; registry admission supplies checkpoint uniqueness. The evidence is local: no deployed registry runs it yet. The registry's fold checks that the AID has no leaf, inserts one, and delivers the checkpoint holding the booking committed. The persistent leaf prevents a second first-registration of the AID, and there is no revival: a registered identity stays live until it is convicted. See the registration guarantee for the atomic mint/insertion obligation and the model's evidence limits.

The new checkpoint's juvenile window starts at born_at, the booking's validity upper bound, which can precede the fold: it is unconsumable until born_at + W, and a fold that lands after that has no juvenile period left. That window is what bounds the stale-key registration above — anyone can advance the checkpoint onward with the controller's later public rotations, and the moment that happens the checkpoint's operative key state is the controller's; the refund address chosen at registration does not change, and a conviction pays the bond still held and the remaining pool to it.

shipped-today_1.text: Advance moves one KERI rotation into the checkpoint. Anyone may relay it because the public event and its receipts determine the only valid successor.

The transaction consumes exactly one current checkpoint and creates exactly one successor with the same quantity-one token, the same complete value, the Cardano sequence increased by one, and the event's keys, thresholds, next commitments, witnesses and toad.
The heavy checks run in observer_advance. They require:
the event to continue from the stored prior event;
revealed keys to match the stored next-key commitments;
both KERI controller thresholds to pass — the event's own and the previously committed next threshold;
signatures to cover the exact rotation bytes;
witness receipts to cover the exact event bytes; and
witness-set changes to satisfy the incoming witness threshold.

When incoming toad is greater than zero, elapsed time and controller signatures never replace the required receipts. This prevents a controller from activating an unpublished Cardano-first branch and repairing the KERI history afterwards.
ixn, dip and drt are rejected: advance requires the type span to read rot.

The validator tallies receipts against the new witness set and the new toad. Whether keripy does the same, or tallies against the parent's set, is not established. Epic #320 builds the oracle that settles it. The two rules disagree exactly on rotations that cut or add witnesses — that is, on witness replacement after a compromise.

under-the-accepted-design_1.text: The predicate is unchanged. What is added is everything around it:
a bond option — keep, or deposit (the unfreeze: refill B after a freeze paid it to the payee the freeze named). There is no withdraw;
the premium P paid from the pool to the payee the transaction names, when the pool covers it. An unpaid rotation is still a valid rotation: no rotation requires the pool to cover the premium;

A deposit travels in a message signed by the keys of the epoch the rotation opens (D-038). A relayer landing the owner's public rotation therefore cannot unfreeze her. Absent means keep. No rotation changes the refund address: it is chosen by whoever pays the registration and fixed for the checkpoint's whole life.

shipped-today_2.text: Close is the controller-authorized retirement path. Its signed evidence binds the network, checkpoint policy, exact checkpoint input reference, AID and current sequence, refund address, and current controller threshold. The transaction consumes the exact checkpoint, satisfies the current weighted threshold, burns the quantity-one token, creates no successor, and refunds the complete remaining value to the signed address.
Binding the input reference makes the authorization single-use. Binding the refund address prevents a transaction builder from redirecting the escrow.

The exposure it leaves. Close answers to the current keys, so a thief who steals them can burn the identity and take the escrow. The signed refund address limits where the money goes but not whether the identity dies.

under-the-accepted-design_2.text: There is no close. The owner keeps her checkpoint alive — bonds, rotations, unfreezing — until it is convicted; a relying party sees a checkpoint that is alive, a pending termination that consumers refuse, or retired once the terminating fold has run. The current-key thief loses the close entirely: the only Cardano power the current keys retain is the poison, and a rotation clears that.

There is no pause, no parking and no revival. Only a conviction is final. Whether an owner who stops maintaining a checkpoint should recover its bonds and pool is an open economic question: today they leave a live checkpoint only through rotation premiums, a freeze and conviction.

shipped-today_3.text: Freeze is a public challenge to a checkpoint that KERI evidence shows is behind. The thin checkpoint requires an observer_enforcement withdrawal, which proves the contested rotation belongs to the same AID, continues from the recorded event, is strictly ahead of the tip, reveals committed keys, satisfies its controller threshold, and carries enough receipts. The checkpoint moves to ARMED — a different role address, so consumers fail closed — with the hunter and a deadline recorded, and the complete escrow preserved.

A response is not an owner-only command: it is the same ordinary advance, applied before the deadline. Evidence is bound to the challenged tip, so after a response the old proof is stale and a new round needs fresh evidence at the new sequence.

under-the-accepted-design_3.text: Freeze survives, with a different job. It is not a punishment for lag — the party who can prove a later witnessed rotation can simply land it, which leaves the checkpoint fresh and costs the owner at most the premium from the pool, so paying for the freeze instead would pay for the harmful move.

Instead a hunter freezes only when the owner's pool is short and the checkpoint is neither frozen nor poisoned: the hunter presents a later witnessed rotation with a freeze attestation for the spent checkpoint, and B goes to the payee the freeze names. The datum changes only its frozen bit to true, so the old keys stay. A depositing rotation clears the bit and restores B. There is no deadline, no claim, no thaw window: the owner comes back by a rotation with deposit, which restores B.
There is no ARMED, no FROZEN role address, no recorded hunter in the datum, and no timeout.

poison-new-in-the-accepted-design.text: Poison — new in the accepted design.

A poison is the current quorum's declaration that this epoch is compromised. The current key quorum authorizes it at cur_threshold; the model does not yet specify the bytes they sign, and no validator implements the poison spend. It is never witnessed, because it is a Cardano-side declaration and not a projected KERI event.

Its effect is one bit. The checkpoint becomes unconsumable. From a poisoned present checkpoint the machine still allows a rotation with its evidence, a top-up while its mark is clear, and a conviction with an eligible commitment; there is no close. A second poison and a freeze are refused — those two require the epoch still clean. Consumer authorization fails because the checkpoint is unconsumable. A rotation clears the poison.
Two properties are worth stating precisely:

The threshold matters. One stolen member key of a k-of-n group cannot poison. In KERI an event signed below threshold is invalid rather than duplicitous, so a single-key poison would assert more than KERI does.

It is epoch-local. Any witnessed rotation clears it, because possession of the next keys is control by KERI's own rule. It serves the window between detection and rotation, and the case of lost next keys where no rotation will ever come. It does not serve next-key theft, where the thief's rotation is control.

convict-new-shape-in-the-accepted-design.text: Convict — new shape in the accepted design.

shipped-today_4.text: convict_predicate accepts a second rotation at the tip's native_sn that reveals exactly the tip's current keys, is signed at cur_threshold, carries receipts from at least toad of the tip's witnesses, and differs in content. It needs no history, because the revealed keys are the current keys. On the shipped machine this burns the token and leaves no successor, and the CLI exposes no command for it.

under-the-accepted-design_4.text: The transaction producing the conviction output must mint both the enforcement and entitlement attestations for the spent checkpoint. The conviction reveals a commitment opened beforehand, within its window and naming this identifier, deployment and key state, together with a rival rotation valid against the same previous commitments; the commitment's payee takes D_reg in full, and the freeze bond still held (none when frozen) and the pool go to the refund address. The checkpoint becomes a pending termination: the output and the token stay, consumers refuse it, and there is no local transition out — no rotate, no poison, no freeze, no top-up (D-030, D-031). A termination booking then moves the pending output into the termination request, and only the fold that consumes that request burns the token and retires the key.

Terminality is not severity. KERI has no event that un-duplicates an identifier: superseding recovery is a rotation over an interaction, by rule and not by duplicity, while two establishment events at one sequence is duplicity and KERI's only answer is permanent distrust. A clearable conviction would be the chain inventing a recovery KERI lacks.

Producing the evidence is narrow: only a holder of the pre-committed keys could have signed the second rotation, and each rotation needs the receipts of its own derived witnesses at its own threshold; the comparison does not itself require the two receipt sets to overlap. Presenting it is not: once the evidence exists, any party that holds the duplicity proof and an eligible commitment can submit the conviction. The residual is real and bounded: a next-key thief with toad colluding witnesses can convict the identity she already controls under KERI and take D_reg on the way out. Exposure is D_reg and the witness set the controller chose.

top-up-new-in-the-accepted-design.text: Top-up — new in the accepted design.

Top-up adds value to the pool, at least one premium P at a time and only once between two rotations. No signature, anyone. It is how a friend, an employer or a consortium pays for an identity's maintenance. A top-up spends the checkpoint output, so a stream of tiny ones could keep the controller's own rotation and the hunters' transactions from landing; the datum therefore carries a top-up mark that a top-up sets and every rotation clears, and a second top-up before the next rotation is refused. Registration asks for the same minimum: the first pool is at least P.

what-is-off-chain.text: The ledger validates the event presented for a transition. It does not:
discover new KERI events by itself;
store or replay the entire KEL;
decide whether an unseen event exists; or
Hunters, controllers and ordinary relayers discover evidence off chain. They do not become trusted authorities: the on-chain validators accept or reject the supplied bytes.
